reason: 'The people began to wax strong in wickedness and abominations.' “wax strong in” occurs in no KJV verse and the past form “waxed strong in” occurs in exactly two, Luke 1:80 and Luke 2:40 — and both of them are the same sentence about a child growing: 'And the child grew, and waxed strong in spirit', said of John the Baptist and then of Jesus. Luke's idiom takes a virtue as its object and describes growth toward a ministry; 3 Nephi 2:3 takes wickedness and abominations as its object and describes a population's decay. 'Wax strong' with an abstract object is ordinary King James English and the Book of Mormon uses it repeatedly on its own account. Recorded because a reader who notices the Luke verses will want to know the catalogue noticed them.

A six-word run and the highest-ranked candidate in this stretch of the chapter, and it is a title. 2 Kings 9:6 is Jehu's anointing — 'I have anointed thee king over the people of the LORD, even over Israel' — and 3 Nephi 2:5 is a dating note: 'since the days of Mosiah, which was king over the people of the Nephites.' Nothing of the anointing scene is present.

The KJV writes out large numbers this way constantly and simply had occasion to write this one at Genesis 11:19. This entry covers the whole run of dating formulas in 2:4-8, which are not listed individually; compare the standing entry at Helaman 1:1.

“which had the charge of” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, which is why the machine ranked it, and the verse is a good deal more interesting than the phrase: Jeremiah 52:25 is the deportation after the fall of Jerusalem, and it lists among the captives 'an eunuch, which had the charge of the men of war' and 'the principal scribe of the host'. A Nephite who had the charge of the records disappearing might be thought to answer that. The best-looking verbal candidate in the chapter and it has to be declined in full, because a reader working with the 1830 text will find it. 1830 reads 'could no where be found in all the land', two words, which 1920 collapsed to 'nowhere' and thereby erased; the first edition preserves the KJV's orthography here as it does at shew and marvellous, and the phrase it preserves is a singleton. “no where” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Samuel 10:14 — Saul's uncle asking where he has been, 'To seek the asses: and when we saw that they were no where'. The sense is nevertheless wrong at every point that matters. 1 Samuel 10:14 is about livestock, and its 'no where' is predicated of the asses, not of a person; 1 Samuel 10:21 is about a man hiding among the stuff who is produced two verses later. Neither is a disappearance, nobody is taken up, and the searches end. 3 Nephi 2:9's man is never produced and the record passes to his son. The link at this verse is filed at 2 Kings 2:17, where the search does fail; this entry records that the sharper verbal candidate was seen, that the 1830 reading is what makes it visible, and that it was refused on sense.

“utter destruction” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 1 Kings 20:42 and Zechariah 14:11, and neither is in view. 1 Kings 20:42 uses it of a man Ahab was to have devoted and let go — the herem, a thing appointed to destruction, not a fate threatened; Zechariah 14:11 promises there shall be no more of it in a restored Jerusalem. 3 Nephi 2:13 uses the phrase as the Book of Mormon uses it everywhere from Alma 9:18 to Helaman 13:10, as a standing term for the annihilation of a people by war. Rare in the KJV, formulaic in this corpus, and a rarity count that measures the King James Bible's vocabulary rather than any borrowing.

A model case for this category, and it needs writing out because the resemblance is at the level of the image and the meaning is exactly reversed. 'Their curse was taken from them, and their skin became white like unto the Nephites.' In the King James Bible a skin turning white is itself the curse and never its removal: Miriam becomes 'leprous, white as snow' for speaking against Moses (Numbers 12:10), Moses's own hand is made 'leprous as snow' as a sign (Exodus 4:6), and Gehazi goes out from Elisha 'a leper as white as snow' for his greed (2 Kings 5:27). “white as snow” occurs in eight KJV verses and the three that describe a human skin are all judgements. There is besides no shared wording — no 'snow', no 'leprous', no 'white as' — and the passage's real antecedents are internal, 2 Nephi 5:21 and Alma 3:6, not biblical. Recorded so that the register shows the catalogue considered the leprosy verses and found the polarity opposed.

A five-word run and the top-ranked candidate for the verse, and the two sentences say opposite things. The pairing of young men with daughters or maidens is one of the KJV's commonest parallelisms and points nowhere by itself.

A five-word run of the plainest causal boilerplate. The construction occurs across the KJV and is the Book of Mormon's default explanation of a military reverse; it recurs in this very chapter at 2:19 ('this because of their iniquity'). No content word is shared beyond 'wickedness'.
